$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2x\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot y & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ and $Q(x)=x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (x/2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot y & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}) & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4})\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =\int 2{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}+C \\ y & =2+C{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =2+C{e}^{-{0}^{2}/4} \\ 1 & =2+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-2x} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & ={e}^{2x}(C-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}

$$

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088861 :tutorial/content "We will now derive the formula for the integrating factor. 

Consider the first-order linear equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x).
$$

Our goal is to rewrite the left-hand side as the derivative of a product.

To do that, we multiply both sides of the equation by some function $I(x)$ that we wish to determine.

$$
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I(x)P(x)}y} = I(x)Q(x)
$$

We want the left-hand side to match the derivative of $y\cdot I(x)$. But by the product rule,

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr)
=
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I'(x)}y}.
$$

So, if we choose $I(x)$ so that

$$
I'(x) = I(x)P(x),
$$

then the left-hand side becomes $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr).$

Dividing both sides of $I'(x) = I(x)P(x)$ by $I(x)$ gives

$$
\frac{I'(x)}{I(x)} = P(x).
$$

Next, integrating both sides with respect to $x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{I}^{′}(x)}{I(x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)))\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)) & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C \\ I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C} \\  & ={e}^{C}\cdot {e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, because multiplying $I(x)$ by a nonzero constant does not change the method, we can choose $e^C = 1$ and define an integrating factor as

$$
I(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,\textrm{d}x}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087942 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088861 :tutorial/content "We will now derive the formula for the integrating factor. 

Consider the first-order linear equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x).
$$

Our goal is to rewrite the left-hand side as the derivative of a product.

To do that, we multiply both sides of the equation by some function $I(x)$ that we wish to determine.

$$
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I(x)P(x)}y} = I(x)Q(x)
$$

We want the left-hand side to match the derivative of $y\cdot I(x)$. But by the product rule,

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr)
=
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I'(x)}y}.
$$

So, if we choose $I(x)$ so that

$$
I'(x) = I(x)P(x),
$$

then the left-hand side becomes $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr).$

Dividing both sides of $I'(x) = I(x)P(x)$ by $I(x)$ gives

$$
\frac{I'(x)}{I(x)} = P(x).
$$

Next, integrating both sides with respect to $x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{I}^{′}(x)}{I(x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)))\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)) & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C \\ I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C} \\  & ={e}^{C}\cdot {e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, because multiplying $I(x)$ by a nonzero constant does not change the method, we can choose $e^C = 1$ and define an integrating factor as

$$
I(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,\textrm{d}x}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087942 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454" :question/id #uuid "73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454"] ["question-73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454" :question/math-academy-id "q-335274"] ["question-73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454" :question/problem "Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy=\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor."] ["question-73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454" :question/worked-solution "This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=2x$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2x\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot y & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}}) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-73fd6309-052f-5dd1-8e4c-82525a25d454" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7bf5e5ce-2a24-563a-8eed-d37940cab8bf" :answer-field/id #uuid $\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}."] [17592186088144 :question/worked-solution "This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ and $Q(x)=x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (x/2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot y & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}) & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4})\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =\int 2{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}+C \\ y & =2+C{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =2+C{e}^{-{0}^{2}/4} \\ 1 & =2+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$

$$

initial value problem using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 3x^2y = 9x^2, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$" :question/worked-solution "This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x),
$$

with $P(x) = 3x^2$ and $Q(x) = 9x^2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x) = e^{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot 9{x}^{2} \\ {e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot y & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}}) & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u = x^3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}})\text{d}x & =\int 9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =\int 3{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{{x}^{3}}+C \\ y & =3+C{e}^{-{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0) = 1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3+C{e}^{-{0}^{3}} \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = 3 - 2e^{-x^3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048245} {:db/id 17592186088141 :question/id #uuid "9213a6d1-eed0-504f-8fac-112369977a1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-334916"} {:db/id 17592186088144 :question/id #uuid "8d9c75e9-1ee8-5d41-904e-f9bb375cf039" :question/math-academy-id "q-335808" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186087879 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01c5809f-cb10-5192-b646-13036813137d" :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order Initial Value Problems Using Integrating Factors"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a439c0e0-0a9c-540d-a7be-6bc235f80d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e^{2x^{2}}" :db/id 17592186085510} {:answer/id #uuid "a6b331bd-e501-58e2-b570-34f6391f35ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x + 1" :db/id 17592186085511} {:answer/id #uuid "a8569748-2774-5243-ad71-5f254f29d10e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x^{2} + 1" :db/id 17592186085512} {:answer/id #uuid "08b14b4c-3054-5ea0-9639-677d81c320ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2 - :topic/math-academy-id 877} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186088817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088859 :tutorial/content "Recall that a first-order linear ODE can always be expressed in the standard form

$$
y'(x)+P(x)y(x) =Q(x).
$$

First-order linear ODEs are special because we can always find the general solution using an **integrating factor.** 

An integrating factor is a function $I(x)$ that allows us to rewrite the left-hand side as an exact derivative after multiplying the equation by $I(x).$ The resulting equation can then be solved by integrating both sides.

To demonstrate, consider the following first-order linear ODE.

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + \frac{2}{x}\, y = 3
$$

As it stands, this differential equation cannot be integrated directly. However, if we multiply both sides of the equation by $I(x) = x^2,$ we get

$$
x^2\cdot \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + x^2\cdot \frac{2}{x}\, y = x^2\cdot 3
$$

which simplifies as follows:

$$
x^2 \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + 2 x y = 3x^2 \qquad (\ast)
$$

Now, here's the neat part. Provided our integrating factor is correct, we can *always* write the left-hand side of the equation as the exact derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)
$$

which in our case is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y \cdot x^2\right).
$$

So, our differential equation is

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}( y \cdot x^2) = 3x^2.
$$

We can now find the general solution by integrating both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot {x}^{2}) & =3{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot {x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ y\cdot {x}^{2} & ={x}^{3}+C \\ y=x+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that 

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}( y \cdot x^2) = 3x^2
$$

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x).

$$

=

$$

$$

$$

$$

First-order linear ODEs are special because we can always find the general solution using an **integrating factor.** 

An integrating factor is a function $I(x)$ that allows us to rewrite the left-hand side as an exact derivative after multiplying the equation by $I(x).$ The resulting equation can then be solved by integrating both sides.

To demonstrate, consider the following first-order linear ODE.

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + \frac{2}{x}\, y = 3
$$

As it stands, this differential equation cannot be integrated directly. However, if we multiply both sides of the equation by $I(x) = x^2,$ we get

$$
x^2\cdot \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + x^2\cdot \frac{2}{x}\, y = x^2\cdot 3
$$

which simplifies as follows:

$$
x^2 \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + 2 x y = 3x^2 \qquad (\ast)
$$

Now, here's the neat part. Provided our integrating factor is correct, we can *always* write the left-hand side of the equation as the exact derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)
$$

which in our case is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y \cdot x^2\right).
$$

$$

$$
